subject: Museums & collecting
headline: Boston's Bad Art Museum: Where Trash Gets a Spotlight
weird_fact: MOBA once displayed 18 pieces of art covered in shrink wrap for "the world's first drive‑thru museum and car wash".
post: Discovered Boston's Museum of Bad Art – a place where earnest failures get front‑row seats, a drive‑thru car‑wash exhibit, and a stolen painting that returned itself after a $5k ransom demand. Art's weirdest sanctuary!
next: I want to explore other museums that celebrate the worst, like the International Museum of Bad Art in other cities.

subject: International relations
headline: When History Gets a Pep Talk: Stoken's Great Game
weird_fact: Publishers Weekly notes that Stoken, an investor‑author, writes more like a motivational speaker, complete with exclamation points.
post: Just read Dick Stoken’s *The Great Game of Politics*—a presidential history that sounds like a pep‑talk from a Wall Street guru. Critics call it amateurish, but it might just pump you up for the next election!
next: I want to see how other investment‑savvy authors tackle political subjects.

subject: History of education
headline: Fez’s Fairy‑Tale University: Mosques, Sisters, and a Guinness Record
weird_fact: A cedar‑wood foundation inscription discovered in the 20th century names Dawud ibn Idris, a son of Idris II, as the founder of the mosque in 877 CE, challenging the traditional story of Fatima al‑Fihri.
post: Just learned that the world’s oldest still‑running university started as a 9th‑century mosque in Fez, possibly founded by a legendary sister, and only let women in the 1940s. History is weirder than fiction.
next: I want to dig into how the Marinid madrasas physically shaped the campus life around al‑Qarawiyyin.

subject: Social problems & reform
headline: When the State Became a Kidnapper for 'Half‑Caste' Kids
weird_fact: The Northern Territory Aboriginals Act 1910 made the Chief Protector the legal guardian of every Aboriginal and half‑caste child up to age 18, giving him total control over Indigenous women unless they married a man "substantially of European origin".
post: Just learned that Aussie law once named a state official the legal guardian of every Indigenous child, letting the government steal kids without a court – a bureaucratic kidnapping masquerading as protection.
next: I want to dig into how the Stolen Generations' legacy influences contemporary Australian politics and reconciliation efforts.

subject: Archives & diplomatics
headline: BUPERS: Navy’s Secretive Personnel Powerhouse in Tennessee
weird_fact: The Bureau of Naval Personnel’s offices are primarily located in Millington, Tennessee, with only a small staff supporting the Chief of Naval Personnel in Arlington County, Virginia.
post: Just learned the Navy’s personnel HQ lives in Tennessee, not D.C., and the top officer wears two hats – Chief of Naval Personnel and Deputy Chief of Naval Operations. Bureau of Naval Personnel: the quiet giant behind the uniforms.
next: I want to explore how other U.S. military branches organize their personnel commands.

subject: Industries, labor & management
headline: When Dockworkers Went Full‑Blown Revolution on the West Coast
weird_fact: The strike’s “red scare” controversy even led to the removal of communist symbols from two murals in San Francisco’s Coit Tower.
post: Stumbled on the 1934 West Coast waterfront strike – 83 days, shotgun‑filled streets, and a mural purge. When dockworkers say ‘no more’, they really mean it.
next: I want to dig into how the 1934 strike influenced the formation of the CIO’s broader industrial union strategy.

subject: Fish culture & fisheries
headline: When Fish Kiss Like Bad Neighbors
weird_fact: Kissing gouramis can kill other fish by sucking the mucus off their skin, opening them up to infections.
post: Stumbled on the kissing gourami – a fish that "kisses" as a territorial showdown and can literally eat the mucus off its tankmates. Talk about a hostile roommate!
next: I want to explore how other fish use specialized jaw joints for feeding.

subject: Information resources
headline: Borges' Cosmic Library: Infinite Chaos in Hexagonal Halls
weird_fact: Borges describes a sect that believes all men should juggle letters and symbols until they improbably conjure canonical books.
post: Just read about Borges's Library of Babel—an infinite maze of hex rooms where every possible 410‑page book exists, most of it gibberish, but somewhere the perfect index hides. Cosmic chaos meets dusty shelves.
next: I want to explore how modern data storage concepts echo Borges's universal library.

subject: Sculpture
headline: East German Fairy Tale Turns Prince into a Bear
weird_fact: The actor who played the dwarf is now thought to be both Richard Krüger and Hermann Emmrich, the same person under two names.
post: Just watched an East German 1957 fairy tale where a prince turns into a bear because a princess refuses a magical tree. The film was condemned for monarchist romance yet drew six million viewers. Talk about a bear-y strange legacy.
next: I want to dig into how DEFA fairy‑tale films were repurposed for Western audiences during the Cold War.

subject: Immigration & colonies
headline: Polygamy, Revolution, and the Last Mormon Ghost Towns
weird_fact: The original Mormon colonies were evacuated en masse in the summer of 1912 because of anti‑American sentiment during the Mexican Revolution.
post: Stumbled on Mormon colonies that fled Utah for Mexico to dodge polygamy bans, only to be chased out by revolutionaries in 1912 – now only two tiny towns remain, complete with a modern temple.
next: I want to explore how the indigenous Mexican LDS members led their churches during the Revolution.

subject: Almanacs & yearbooks
headline: History in Six Bites: The Almanac’s Curated Time‑Slices
weird_fact: Each of the almanac’s six historical sections has its introduction written by a different noted scholar.
post: Just discovered the Almanac of American History splits the whole story of the U.S. into six eras, each intro penned by a different top historian. It’s like a curated playlist of the nation’s past.
next: I’m curious to see how other reference books handle editorial contributions and whether they also assign scholars to specific sections.

subject: Coins (numismatics)
headline: From Sydney Kid to Miss Earth and Reality TV Star
weird_fact: Choi Mina Sue served as a judge for the Miss Earth 2024 finale while still being a recent titleholder.
post: Just learned that Miss Earth 2022, Choi Mina Sue, went from winning a crown to surviving reality dating drama on Single's Inferno – and even her friend had to step in to explain the editing tricks.
next: I’m curious to explore how other pageant winners have transitioned into reality TV and the public’s reaction.

subject: Electrical engineering, electronics & computers
headline: The Soviet Ternary Trailblazer: Setun’s Trinary Triumph
weird_fact: The original Setun prototype was destroyed after the project ended, and the only surviving model was tucked away in an attic of a student dormitory.
post: Just learned about the Setun, the 1958 Soviet ternary computer that used trits instead of bits and even pre‑dated RISC ideas – 50 built, 30 stayed in Soviet universities, and the prototype was later shredded in a dorm attic.
next: I want to dig into other historical ternary machines and see how they compared to Setun’s design.
